opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a fun question, because the answer has changed a lot as the scale has changed. When you're building a network for a few thousand GPUs, you can borrow a lot from how we've built data center networks for the last couple of decades. Once you get into tens or hundreds of thousands of accelerators all working on a single training job, the assumptions start to break.

The first thing I think about is that the network isn't a separate system sitting next to the compute. It's part of the computer. In a traditional data center, you have lots of independent workloads and statistical multiplexing smooths everything out. In a large training run, you have one giant synchronous program, and the whole job moves at the speed of the slowest link. So tail latency and consistency matter much more than average throughput. One flaky optic or one congested switch port can slow down the whole cluster.

That leads to a few design principles. One is that you design around failure, not around the absence of failure. At this scale something is always broken. A cable is degrading, a transceiver is throwing errors, a host has a bad NIC. The network has to detect that quickly, route around it, and give the training stack enough signal to react, whether that's checkpointing, swapping in spare capacity, or rerouting traffic. A lot of the real engineering work is observability and fast diagnosis rather than raw bandwidth.

Another is co-design with the workload. The communication patterns in training aren't random. You know you're going to do all-reduces, all-to-alls for mixture-of-experts, pipeline sends between stages. If you understand those patterns, you can shape the topology, the collective algorithms, and even how you place parts of the model on the hardware so the heaviest traffic stays on the fastest, most local links. Network people, systems people, and researchers have to actually talk to each other, because a choice in the model architecture can completely change what the network needs to do.

Then there's the physical reality: power, cooling, how far signals can travel over copper versus optics, how many tiers of switching you need, and what that does to cost and reliability. Every extra hop and every extra optic is something that can fail and something that burns power. So there's constant tension between building something flat, simple, and high bandwidth, and building something you can actually deploy, power, and maintain on a reasonable timeline.

And finally, I try to keep things as simple as possible. It's tempting to add clever mechanisms at every layer, but at huge scale, complexity becomes a source of failures you can't debug. The designs that hold up best are the ones where, when something goes wrong at 3 a.m., you can figure out what happened.

r001.rationale: The response discusses tail latency and congestion, but does not state that without MRC, spreading fixed aggregate bandwidth across more paths worsens the tail of the load distribution.

r002.rationale: The response does not explain that deterministic routing prevents load imbalances that would otherwise need a corrective feedback loop.

r003.rationale: It calls for co-designing the network with the workload, including topology, collective algorithms, and model placement, and says model architecture can change network requirements.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I think about scaling networks for AI, the first thing I try to do is separate the problem into layers and ask, at each layer, what's actually the binding constraint.

At the bottom you've got physics. Moving bits across copper versus optics, the power per bit, the reach you can get before signal integrity falls apart. Those numbers set hard limits on how dense a rack can be and how far apart your accelerators can sit. A lot of the interesting design work happens right there, because if you can move a little more traffic over electrical links inside a rack, you save a lot of power and cost compared to lighting up optics everywhere.

Above that is topology. Training workloads are not like general data center traffic. They're very synchronized, very bursty, and the collective operations, your all-reduces and all-to-alls, have predictable patterns. So you can design the fabric around those patterns rather than for arbitrary any-to-any traffic. That's why you see people building scale-up domains that are extremely high bandwidth and low latency, and then a separate scale-out network that's optimized for a different set of tradeoffs. Deciding where that boundary sits is one of the most consequential choices you make.

Then there's the question of what happens when something breaks. At tens of thousands of accelerators, something is always failing. A link flaps, an optic degrades, a switch reboots. If a single slow link stalls a synchronous step across the whole cluster, your effective utilization falls off a cliff. So resilience and tail latency become first-class design goals, not afterthoughts. You want the fabric to route around problems quickly and you want the software stack to tolerate it.

And honestly, the thing that ties it together is co-design. The network, the accelerator, the collective communication library, and the model parallelism strategy all have to be designed with knowledge of each other. If the networking team builds something in isolation, the software team will find the corner cases within a week. So we spend a lot of time asking what the model actually needs to communicate and when, and then working backwards to the hardware.

r001.rationale: The response discusses bandwidth, topology, and tail latency, but does not state that spreading fixed aggregate bandwidth across more paths worsens the tail of the load distribution without MRC.

r002.rationale: It mentions designing the fabric around predictable collective patterns and routing around failures, but does not explain deterministic routing preventing load imbalance or the need for a corrective feedback loop.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says the network, accelerator, collective communication library, and model-parallelism strategy must be co-designed, describing hardware and workload design as interdependent for scaling.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing is that you have to design the network around the workload. How much communication does the computation require, when does that communication happen, and how much of it can you overlap with useful work? Those questions tell you where bandwidth and latency actually matter.

As you scale, it becomes a system design problem. You can have very fast individual links and still spend a lot of time waiting if the topology or the way you distribute the computation creates bottlenecks. So you want to think about the compute, the network, and the software together.

And reliability becomes a first-class consideration. The larger the system, the more you have to expect that some component will be unavailable or performing poorly. The goal is to keep the overall system productive through those failures. Ultimately, I’d judge the design by how much useful computation it enables, rather than just the peak numbers of its individual components.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention MRC, fixed aggregate bandwidth, or how adding paths affects the tail of the load distribution.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss deterministic routing or preventing imbalances that would require a corrective feedback loop.

r003.rationale: It says compute, network, and software should be considered together, but does not identify vertical integration between network hardware and workload design as necessary to push scale limits.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to treat it as a whole-system design problem. You can’t make decisions about compute, memory, networking, and software independently, because at larger scales those choices become tightly coupled. Adding more chips only helps if you can keep them doing useful work.

So I’d start with the workload: how much communication does it require, how much data needs to move, and where are the bottlenecks? That helps you decide where to invest in bandwidth, how to organize the network, and how to schedule the work. And as the system grows, reliability becomes part of performance—you need to be able to handle failures without losing the benefit of all that scale.

The goal is useful throughput, rather than just a bigger machine. Sometimes that means making an individual component more powerful, and sometimes it means making the pieces work together more efficiently.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention MRC, fixed aggregate bandwidth, more network paths, or a worsening tail in load distribution.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss deterministic routing, preventing load imbalances, or avoiding a corrective feedback loop.

r003.rationale: It describes compute, networking, software, and workload as coupled, but does not clearly identify vertical integration between network hardware and workload design as necessary to push AI system scale.
